Trito is a mythical figure

== Body ==
To the third man Trito, the celestial gods then offer cattle as a divine gift, which is stolen by a three-headed [[Proto-Indo-European mythology#Serpent-slaying myth|serpent]] named *''{{PIE|Ngʷhi}}'' ("serpent"; and the Indo-European root for [[Affirmation and negation|negation]]). Trito first suffers at his hands, but the hero eventually manages to overcome the monster, fortified by an intoxicating drink and aided by the Sky-Father. He eventually gives the recovered cattle back to a priest for it to be properly sacrificed.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=58}} Trito is now the first warrior, maintaining through his heroic actions the cycle of mutual giving between gods and mortals.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=63–64}}

==== Interpretations ====
According to Lincoln, Manu and Yemo seem to be the protagonists of "a myth of the sovereign function, establishing the model for later priests and kings", while the legend of Trito should be interpreted as "a myth of the warrior function, establishing the model for all later men of arms".{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=63–64}} The myth indeed recalls the [[Georges Dumézil|Dumézilian]] [[Trifunctional hypothesis|tripartition]] of the cosmos between the priest (in both his magical and legal aspects), the warrior (the Third Man), and the herder (the cow).{{sfn|Anthony|2007|pp=134–135}}

The story of Trito served as a model for later [[cattle raiding]] epic myths and most likely as a moral justification for the practice of raiding among Indo-European peoples. In the original legend, Trito is only taking back what rightfully belongs to his people, those who sacrifice properly to the gods.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=63–64}} The myth has been interpreted either as a cosmic conflict between the heavenly hero and the earthly serpent, or as an Indo-European victory over non-Indo-European people, the monster symbolizing the aboriginal thief or usurper.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|pp=58, 62}}

[[Cognate|Cognates]] deriving from the Proto-Indo-European First Priest ''*Manu'' ("[[Human|Man]]", "ancestor of mankind") include the Indic [[Manu (Hinduism)|Manu]], legendary first man in [[Hinduism]], and Manāvī, his sacrificed wife; the Germanic [[Mannus]] ([[Proto-Germanic language|PGmc]] ''*Mannaz''), mythical ancestor of the [[West Germanic languages|West Germanic tribes]]; and the Persian Manūščihr (from [[Avestan|Aves.]] ''Manūš.čiθra''), a [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrian]] high priest of the 9th century AD.{{Sfn|Mallory|Adams|1997|p=367}} From the name of the sacrificed First King ''*Yemo'' ("Twin") derive the Indic [[Yama]], god of death and the underworld; the [[Avestan]] [[Jamshid|Yima]], king of the golden age and guardian of hell; the [[Norse mythology|Norse]] [[Ymir]] (from PGmc *''Jumijaz''), ancestor of the giants ([[Jötunn|''jötnar'']]); and most likely [[Romulus and Remus|Remus]] (from Proto-Latin ''*Yemos'' or ''*Yemonos'', with the initial ''y''- shifting to ''r''- under the [[Linguistic contamination|influence]] of ''Rōmulus''), killed in the [[Founding of Rome|Roman foundation myth]] by his twin brother [[Romulus]].{{Sfn|Lincoln|1975|p=129}} Cognates stemming from the First Warrior ''*Trito'' ("Third") include the Vedic [[Trita]], the Avestan [[Fereydun|Thrita]], and the Norse [[þriði]].{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=47}}

The motif of Manu and Yemo has been influential throughout Eurasia following the [[Indo-European migrations]]. The Greek, Old Russian (''Poem on the Dove King'') and Jewish versions depend on the Iranian, and a Chinese version of the myth has been introduced from Ancient India.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1975|p=125}} The Armenian version of the myth of the First Warrior Trito depends on the Iranian, and the Roman reflexes were influenced by earlier Greek versions.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=46}}<!--End Content from [[Proto-Indo-European mythology]]-->

== Historiography ==
Following a first paper on the cosmogonical legend of Manu and Yemo, published simultaneously with [[Jaan Puhvel]] in 1975 (who pointed out the Roman reflex of the story), [[Bruce Lincoln]] assembled the initial part of the myth with the legend of the third man Trito in a single ancestral motif.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|pp=42–43}}{{sfn|Anthony|2007|pp=134–135}}{{Sfn|Mallory|Adams|2006|pp=435–436}}

Since the 1970s, the reconstructed motifs of Manu and Yemo, and to a lesser extent that of Trito, have been generally accepted among scholars.<ref>See: {{harvnb|Puhvel|1987|pp=285–287}}; {{harvnb|Mallory|Adams|2006|pp=435–436}}; {{harvnb|Anthony|2007|pp=134–135}}. {{harvnb|West|2007}} agrees with the reconstructed motif of Manu and Yemo, although he notes that interpretations of the myths of [[Trita]] and [[Fereydun|Thraētona]] are debated. According to {{Harvard citation no brackets|Polomé|1986}}, "some elements of the [Scandinavian myth of Ymir] are distinctively Indo-Europeans", but the reconstruction of the creation myth of the first Man and his Twin proposed by {{Harvard citation no brackets|Lincoln|1975}} "makes too unprovable assumptions to account for the fundamental changes implied by the Scandinavian version".</ref>

=== First Warrior ===
To the third man Trito, the celestial gods offer cattle as a divine gift, which is stolen by a three-headed [[Proto-Indo-European mythology#Serpent-slaying myth|serpent]] named *''{{PIE|Ng<sup>w</sup>hi}}'' ('serpent'; and the Indo-European root for [[Affirmation and negation|negation]]).{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=51}}{{sfn|Anthony|2007|pp=134–135}}

Trito first suffers at his hands, but fortified by an intoxicating drink and aided by a helper-god (the [[Perkwunos|Storm-God]] or ''*H<sub>a</sub>ner'', 'Man'),{{sfn|Anthony|2007|pp=134–135}}{{snf|Mallory|Adams|2006|p=437}} together they go to a cave or a mountain, and the hero finally manages to overcome the monster. Trito then gives the recovered cattle back to a priest for it to be properly sacrificed.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=58}}{{sfn|Anthony|2007|pp=134–135}}{{snf|Mallory|Adams|1997|p=138}} He is now the first warrior, maintaining through his heroic deeds the cycle of mutual giving between gods and mortals.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|pp=63–64}}{{sfn|Anthony|2007|pp=134–135}}

=== Three Functions ===
According to Lincoln, Manu and Yemo seem to be the protagonists of "a myth of the sovereign function, establishing the model for later priests and kings", while the legend of Trito should be seen as "a myth of the warrior function, establishing the model for all later men of arms".{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|pp=63–64}} He has thus interpreted the narrative as an expression of the priests's and kings's attempt to justify their role as indispensable for the preservation of the cosmos, and therefore as essential for the organization of society.{{Sfn|Arvidsson|2006|p=302}} The motif indeed recalls the [[Georges Dumézil|Dumézilian]] [[Trifunctional hypothesis|tripartition]] of the cosmos between the priest (in both his magical and legal aspects), the warrior (the Third Man), and the herder (the cow).{{sfn|Anthony|2007|pp=134–135}}

=== Trito and Ng<sup>w</sup>hi ===
[[Cognate|Cognates]] stemming from the First Warrior ''*Trito'' ('Third') include the Vedic [[Trita]], the hero who recovered the stolen cattle from the serpent [[Vritra|Vṛtrá]]; the Avestan [[Fereydun|Thraētona]] ('son of Thrita'), who won back the abducted women from the serpent [[Zahhak|Aži Dahāka]]; and the Norse [[þriði]] ('Third'), one of the [[List of names of Odin|names of Óðinn]].{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|pp=47–48}}{{Sfn|West|2007|p=260}}{{snf|Mallory|Adams|1997|page=138}} Other cognates may appear in the Greek expressions ''trítos sōtḗr'' (τρίτος σωτήρ; 'Third Saviour'), an epithet of [[Zeus]], and ''tritogḗneia'' (τριτογήνεια; 'Third born' or 'born of Zeus'), an epithet of [[Athena]]; and perhaps in the Slavic mythical hero ''Troyan'', found in Russian and Serbian legends alike.{{Sfn|West|2007|p=260}}{{efn|''Troyan'' has been tentatively connected to numeral "try" 'three', [[Ukrainian language|Ukrainian]] ''troian'' 'father of triplets/three sons', or considered a possible guardian deity of Russia in pre-Christian times.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Bilaniuk |first=Petro B. T. |title=The Ultimate Reality and Meaning in the Pre-Christian Religion of the Eastern Slavs |journal=Ultimate Reality and Meaning |volume=11 |issue=4 |date=December 1988 |pages=254, 258–259 |doi=10.3138/uram.11.4.247}}</ref>}}

''*Ng<sup>w</sup>hi'', a term meaning 'serpent', is also related to the Indo-European root for negation (''*ne-'').{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=51}}{{sfn|Anthony|2007|pp=134–135}} Descendent cognates can be found in the Iranian ''Aži'', the name of the inimical serpent, and in the Indic ''áhi'' ('serpent'), a term used to designate the monstrous serpent [[Vritra|Vṛtrá]],{{Sfn|West|2007|p=260}} both descending from [[Proto-Indo-Iranian language|Proto-Indo-Iranian]] ''*aj'hi''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Witzel |first=Michael |title=In Hot Pursuit of Language in Prehistory, Essays in the Four Fields of Anthropology |date=2008 |publisher=John Benjamins Publishing |isbn=9789027232526 |editor-last=Bengtson |editor-first=John D. |pages=269 |chapter=Slaying the Dragon across Eurasia}}</ref>

== Parallels and legacy ==
The motif of Manu and Yemo has been influential throughout Eurasia following the [[Indo-European migrations]]. The Greek, Old Russian (''Poem on the Dove King'') and Jewish versions depend on the Iranian, and a Chinese version of the myth has been introduced from Ancient India.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1975|p=125}} The Armenian version of the myth of the First Warrior Trito depends on the Iranian, and the Roman reflexes were influenced by earlier Greek versions.{{Sfn|Lincoln|1976|p=46}}
